name: Basalt Grey
lede: Basalt Grey is a dark, cool grey standardized by RAL, and under Werner's 1814 naturalist's system the same hue was pinned to a beetle's wing case and the mineral serpentine.

sections.title: A grey pinned to a beetle and a stone
sections.body:
The library dates Basalt Grey to RAL colors 7011 and 7012, both approximate screen values, and to the ISCC-NBS block 113 of 1955 [1]. Werner's system, read from an aged swatch and treated as approximate, assigns a close match to the elytra (wing cases) of the beetle *Meloe violaceus* and to dark streaks on cayenne pepper leaves [1]. It also ties the same match to the mineral serpentine, and names it Blackish Green there, a name the library grades a near-duplicate rather than the same color [1].

The nearest named colors on file are [[slate-color]], [[slate-grey]], [[slate-grey]] and [[blue-slate]], at 3.1, 3.5, 3.5 and 3.8 ΔE [1]. The library's closest recorded neighbor is Iron Grey, about 1.9 units away [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this grey in 777 of 23,781 paintings, 3.3 percent, as photographed [2]. The earliest dated match, Saint John the Evangelist by the Master of Saint Francis, is from 1272, more than six centuries before either the RAL or Werner records, a floor and not a first, since the archive's early centuries are thin [2]. It peaks in the 1930s, at 3.1 times the archive's overall rate, and Henri Matisse carries it in 14 of his 50 paintings here, well above his own museums' baseline [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays a mid-tone, in 54 percent of its appearances [2].
